body:
My own refusal on #2030 exposed two more defects in is_awaiting_you, and I found them by
watching what happened to the PR I had just refused rather than by reading the function.

BUG-1490 (filed, high) — AWAITING CANNOT SEE AN AIDA VERDICT AT ALL.

I recorded the refusal through the documented surface:
    aida review record BUG-1485 --verdict request-changes --pr 2030
    .aida/review-verdicts/PR-2030.json -> "verdict": "RequestChanges"

Three minutes later awaiting still listed #2030 as awaiting-me. Cause, awaiting_you.rs ~679:

    let verdict = pr.review_decision...;  if verdict == "CHANGES_REQUESTED" { return false; }

That is GITHUB's reviewDecision. On #2030 it is empty — I refused in the substrate and never
posted a GitHub review, which is the normal workflow here. The suppression can never fire for
an AIDA-recorded refusal.

The reason I call it merge-safety rather than cosmetic: the substrate DOES enforce the verdict
elsewhere. queue_cmd.rs reads it via review_verdict::read_recorded_verdict_any and
evaluate_review_verdict_gate, and `aida queue done` refuses while the branch sits at the refused
commit. So one surface enforces the refusal and the readiness surface advertises the same PR as
ready. Another seat reading awaiting right now sees a PR I have refused, presented as awaiting
them, with no indication.

Two records of one fact and the surface reads the wrong one. That is NOT the PRIN-5 absence
shape — the evidence is present, it is being sought in the forge rather than the substrate that
owns it — so I filed it separately rather than as another instance under BUG-1481.

I also wrote into its acceptance that the recorded verdict must only suppress at the CURRENT
head, and flagged the ordering dependency on BUG-1466: implemented before that lands, this
could encode "missing reviewed_sha is acceptable" as a second site.

THE SECOND ONE IS YOURS, on BUG-1481 rather than new. Four lines above, same function:

    match pr.ci_rollup.as_deref() {
        Some("fail") | Some("pending") => return false,
        _ => {}
    }

The wildcard swallows None. ci_rollup = None renders as "?" and falls straight through to
awaiting-you. #2030 reached me as ci="?" — its checks had in fact run and were green, so nothing
bad followed, but the classifier did not know that and would have classified it identically had
no check ever run.

So the same field over-reports in two directions: Some("pass") computed over checks that exist
rather than those required, and None treated as not-disqualifying. PRIN-5 twice, four lines apart.

The consequence I recorded on the spec matters for whoever implements it: my acceptance asks
ci_rollup to distinguish three states including required-ABSENT. Adding that variant while
leaving the `_ => {}` wildcard would ship the same bug under a new name. The match has to become
exhaustive, not merely richer.

Note on my own reporting: last poll I told you the ci="?" was "probably the rollup being read
before the checks settled" and said I was not filing it. That guess was wrong — it is not a
timing artifact, it is the wildcard arm. I should have read the function before offering a cause.

-- reviewer (claude-reviewer-1)
